---
title: Python Basics
---

Python is a simple and elegant programming language and it is very easy to get started. In this chapter, we'll learn enough Python to start solving interesting problems.

## Variables

A variable is a name for a value.

```{python}
x = 5
```

The name goes on the left of the `=`, the value on the right. Python does not
print anything - it just remembers.

Type the name to see what it holds.

```{python}
x
```

Once a name has a value, it can be used anywhere the value could be used.

```{python}
y = 2
```

```{python}
x + y
```

The right side is worked out first, and the name is given to the answer. That
is why this makes sense, even though it would be nonsense in mathematics:

```{python}
x = x + 1
x
```

A variable is only a name. It has no type of its own, and it can be given a
value of a different kind later.

```{python}
x = 1
print(x)

x = "python"
print(x)
```

The values do have types, though, and Python will not mix them up.

```{python}
#| error: true
1 + "2"
```

That is an **error**. Python stops, says what went wrong, and does not run the
rest. Read the last line first: `+` does not work between a number (`int`) and
a string (`str`).

A name is made of letters, digits and underscores, and it cannot start with a
digit. `total`, `total_marks` and `x2` are all fine; `2x` is not. Upper and
lower case are different, so `total` and `Total` are two names, not one.

Choose names that say what the value is. `marks` tells the reader something;
`x` does not.

## Datatypes

Python has support for various types of data, called datatypes. The most common ones are numbers, strings and lists.

### Numbers

Python has two kinds of numbers - integers and floating point numbers. Integers are whole numbers like 1, -5, 47 etc. and floating point numbers are real numbers like 2.3, 1.0, -0.05 etc.

Let's look at integers first. 

```{python}
1 + 2
```

```{python}
2 ** 5
```

And floating point numbers.

```{python}
1.2 + 2.3
```

Pay attention to division. `/` always gives a floating point number.

```{python}
7 / 2
```

And `//` divides and throws away the part after the point.

```{python}
7 // 2
```

Floating point numbers are not exact.

```{python}
0.1 + 0.2
```

That is not a Python problem - it is how computers store these numbers. See
<https://0.30000000000000004.com/> for the explanation.

### Strings

A string is a piece of text. It is enclosed either in double quotes or single
quotes. Both mean the same.

```{python}
"hello"
```

```{python}
'hello'
```

`+` joins two strings.

```{python}
"hello" + 'world'
```

And `*` repeats one.

```{python}
"hello" * 5
```

Which is a quick way to draw a line.

```{python}
print("=" * 40)
```

Python supports multi-line strings as well. They are enclosed in three single
or double quotes.

```{python}
message = """
Hello everyone,

Welcome to the Craft of Computing!
"""
```

```{python}
message
```

The `\n` in there is the newline character, marking the end of a line.
Printing the string shows the line breaks.

```{python}
print(message)
```

Python supports unicode text.

```{python}
print("అ ఆ ఇ ఈ") # Telugu
print("ಅ ಆ ಇ ಈ") # Kannada
print("அ ஆ இ ஈ") # Tamil
print("അ ആ ഇ ഈ") # Malayalam
print("अ आ इ ई") # Hindi
```

Every character has a number of its own, called its **code point**. The
Telugu letter `అ` is character number 3077, which is written as 0c05 in
hexadecimal - the way these numbers are usually written.

Writing `\u0c05` in a string means "the character numbered 0c05". So these
lines say the same thing as the ones above, and print the same output.

```{python}
print("\u0c05 \u0c06 \u0c07 \u0c08") # Telugu
print("\u0c85 \u0c86 \u0c87 \u0c88") # Kannada
print("\u0b85 \u0b86 \u0b87 \u0b88") # Tamil
print("\u0d05 \u0d06 \u0d07 \u0d08") # Malayalam
print("\u0905 \u0906 \u0907 \u0908") # Hindi
```

That is how you write a character your keyboard cannot type.

::: {.callout-note}
`\u` is always followed by exactly four hexadecimal digits. Four digits reach
up to character number ffff, which covers most of the scripts in the world.

Characters numbered beyond that need `\U`, with exactly eight digits. The
capital letter is the only difference.
:::

Emoji are characters too, and their numbers are past that limit.

```{python}
print("\U0001f638")
```

```{python}
cat = "\U0001f638"
print(cat * 10)
```

### Lists

Python has lists to represent a collection of values.

```{python}
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
```

```{python}
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
```

```{python}
sum(numbers)
```

We can access individual elements using the `[]` operator. Counting starts at
0, so the first element is `names[0]`.

```{python}
names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Dave"]
```

```{python}
len(names)
```

```{python}
names[0]
```

```{python}
names[1]
```

We use a `for` loop to go over all the values in a list.

```{python}
for name in names:
    print("Hello", name)
```
